sources.quote:
Classify the final execution context before assessing impact:<sup>[[8]](#references)[[9]](#references)</sup>
 Context | What successful injection normally gains | What to verify |
 Host-page DOM modified by a content script | JavaScript in the web page's main world, not automatic access to the content script's isolated-world privileges | Page CSP and whether a DOM or window.postMessage bridge forwards attacker data to the content script |
 Ordinary extension page (popup, options page, or reachable extension HTML) | The extension origin and the extension APIs available to that page | The extension-page CSP, manifest permissions, and any runtime-message handlers reachable from the page |
 Manifest V2 background page | A privileged extension page with a DOM | Whether attacker data reaches an HTML/code-execution sink through messaging or stored state |
 Manifest V3 service worker | No DOM, so this is a message/API or code-injection review rather than DOM XSS | Untrusted messages, unsafe URL/API arguments, and dynamic-code sinks |
 Page listed in sandbox.pages | Script allowed by the sandbox's separate CSP, but in a unique origin without extension APIs or direct access to non-sandboxed pages | Whether a privileged parent trusts messages from the sandbox and exposes an unsafe postMessage bridge |

The sandbox case is an important exception to the usual MV3 CSP rule.

items.claim: Reflection alone is not a cross-site scripting finding when the reflected payload sits in the body of a 302: the browser never renders that body, so the injection only counts once it lands somewhere the browser actually parses.

Reflection alone is not a cross-site scripting finding when the reflected payload sits in the body of a 302: the browser never renders that body, so the injection only counts once it lands somewhere the browser actually parses.

HackTricks reference: XSS (Cross Site Scripting) (pentesting-web/xss-cross-site-scripting/README.md)
items.disproof: Script executing from a payload delivered only in the body of a 302 response, in a browser that follows the redirect before parsing, refutes this claim.

sources.quote: This is not trivial as modern browsers do not interpret the HTTP response body if the HTTP response status code is a 302, so just a cross-site scripting payload is useless.

The CSP directive can specify a nonce (a random value) and the same value must be used in the tag that loads a script. If the values do not match, then the script will not execute. To be effective as a control, the nonce must be securely generated on each page load and not be guessable by an attacker. The CSP directive can specify a hash of the contents of the trusted script. If the hash of the actual script does not match the value specified in the directive, then the script will not execute. If the content of the script ever changes, then you will of course need to update the hash value

Shadow Workers is a command-and-control framework dedicated to service-worker exploitation.<sup>[[4]](#references)</sup>

Service-worker update checks bypass the browser cache when the previous fetch occurred more than 24 hours ago, but that does not guarantee that a malicious worker disappears within 24 hours: the old worker can remain active until a changed script is fetched, installed, and activated.

DOM-based XSS vulnerabilities usually arise when JavaScript takes data from an attacker-controllable source, such as the URL, and passes it to a sink that supports dynamic code execution, such as eval() or innerHTML . This enables attackers to execute malicious JavaScript, which typically allows them to hijack other users' accounts. To deliver a DOM-based XSS attack, you need to place data into a source so that it is propagated to a sink and causes execution of arbitrary JavaScript. The most common source for DOM XSS is the URL, which is typically accessed with the window.location object

items.claim: Service-worker XSS is only reachable when two prerequisites line up: a place to serve attacker JavaScript from the target origin, either a file upload or a JSONP endpoint whose output can be filled with arbitrary JS, plus an XSS that can load and register that script as the worker.
items.body:
Service-worker XSS is only reachable when two prerequisites line up: a place to serve attacker JavaScript from the target origin, either a file upload or a JSONP endpoint whose output can be filled with arbitrary JS, plus an XSS that can load and register that script as the worker.

HackTricks reference: Abusing Service Workers (pentesting-web/xss-cross-site-scripting/abusing-service-workers.md)
items.disproof: Registering and controlling a worker script on the origin with neither arbitrary-JS hosting nor a JSONP endpoint that can be made to emit arbitrary JS refutes these as the required prerequisites.

sources.quote:
Attack Creating a Service Worker

In order to exploit this vulnerability you need to find:

- A way to upload arbitrary JS files to the server and a XSS to load the service worker of the uploaded JS file
- A vulnerable JSONP request where you can manipulate the output (with arbitrary JS code) and a XSS to load the JSONP with a payload that will load a malicious service worker.
